Read About Cartagena

Walled, layered, and impossible to reduce — Cartagena carries five centuries of Spanish empire, slave trade, independence, and Caribbean light inside a single city center.

The Port That Moved the World

When Spain needed a gateway to its South American empire, it chose this bay. Cartagena de Indias was founded in 1533 on a sheltered harbor where the mountains of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta are visible on clear days to the northeast, and the Colombian coast curves inward to create a natural anchorage. Within decades it had become the most important port in the Americas. Silver from the Peruvian mines at Potosí, gold from New Granada, emeralds from Muzo — all of it moved through Cartagena's docks on its way to Seville. The wealth was so concentrated and so visible that the city became the most attacked port in the New World, targeted repeatedly by English, French, and Dutch privateers. Drake sacked it in 1586 and had to be paid a ransom to leave.

The Spanish response was the most ambitious fortification project in the Americas. Over two centuries they built a complete circuit of walls around the old city, constructed the Castillo de San Felipe de Barajas on the hill above, and linked the outlying fortifications with a chain of gun emplacements designed to catch any attacker in crossfire. The system worked. In 1741, British Admiral Vernon arrived with a fleet of 186 ships and 23,000 men — the largest naval assault in American history to that point — and was driven back by a Spanish garrison one-tenth that size. The victory became one of the founding stories of Colombian national identity, the moment the city proved it could hold.

The Walls and What They Enclosed

The walls that circle the old city today are largely the ones that repelled Vernon in 1741. They are between nine and seventeen meters high in places, wide enough to drive a vehicle along the top, and made from a coral limestone called sillar that turns warm gold in afternoon light. They were not built all at once — construction began in the 1630s, continued for most of the colonial period, and was repeatedly modified after each attack revealed weaknesses. The result is a structure that records its own history in its dimensions and angles. Some sections are older and thicker; some are later additions that patched gaps. The whole circuit is about eleven kilometers long.

Walking the walls at dusk, when the heat has broken and the Caribbean light goes flat and golden, is one of those experiences that makes everything you read about a place suddenly feel proportional.

Inside the walls, the street grid follows the colonial logic of a city designed for hierarchy and administration. The cathedral faces its own plaza. The Palacio de la Inquisición, where the Holy Office operated from 1610 to 1821, sits on the same square. The merchant houses of the trading families occupy the interior blocks, their balconies projecting over the narrow streets, heavy with bougainvillea. The scale is deliberately compressed — everything important is within walking distance of everything else, which was the point in a city meant to concentrate power and tax it efficiently.

San Basilio de Palenque and the Other Story

The wealth flowing through Cartagena was built on enslaved people. The port received a significant portion of the Africans brought to Spanish South America — estimates suggest between 100,000 and 150,000 enslaved people passed through Cartagena between 1533 and the early nineteenth century. They came primarily from the Senegambia region, the Gold Coast, and what is now Angola, and they carried languages, spiritual practices, and forms of social organization that survived the passage and the plantation system, often in forms the Spanish colonial administration could not fully control.

The most dramatic form that resistance took was the palenque — a fortified community established by escaped slaves in the mountains and forests outside colonial control. San Basilio de Palenque, about seventy kilometers southeast of Cartagena, was founded in the early seventeenth century by an enslaved man named Benkos Bióho after he escaped and organized a sustained guerrilla campaign against the colonial authorities. In 1691, the Spanish signed a peace treaty recognizing San Basilio as a free community — the first free African town in the Americas. The community has survived to the present. Its language, Palenquero — a Spanish-based creole that incorporates Bantu grammatical structures and vocabulary — is still spoken there and was designated by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2005.

In Cartagena itself, you can find traces of this history in the vendors who sell sweets in the old city carrying baskets on their heads — a practice that connects back to enslaved women who supplemented their survival by selling food in the streets. The connection is not commemorated the way the colonial architecture is, but it is present if you look for it.

Independence and What Followed

Cartagena declared independence from Spain on November 11, 1811 — the first city in what is now Colombia to do so, and it celebrates this date as its defining civic moment. The path from declaration to actual independence was not direct. Spanish forces reconquered the city in 1815 after a brutal siege known as the Reconquista that killed an estimated six thousand residents through starvation and disease. The city's population, which had been around seventeen thousand, collapsed to around nine thousand in the aftermath.

Simón Bolívar's campaigns eventually drove the Spanish out for good in 1821. But the liberation brought its own complications. Cartagena lost its position as the premier port of South America over the following decades as the Magdalena River silted up at its mouth and trade routes shifted. Bogotá rose as the center of national power. The city that had been the most important in the Americas declined into a secondary regional port, which — from a certain angle — preserved it. The colonial center was never torn down and rebuilt because there was not the economic pressure to do so. What had been neglect became, in the twentieth century, an asset.

Gabriel García Márquez's Caribbean

Gabriel García Márquez was born in Aracataca, a small town in the banana zone of Magdalena department, in 1927. He grew up on the Caribbean coast and spent significant portions of his life in Bogotá and Mexico City, but his imagination remained permanently anchored to this coast — its heat, its superstitions, its smell of salt and decay, its way of treating the marvelous as ordinary. Cartagena and the fictional Macondo, the village at the center of One Hundred Years of Solitude, are different places, but they draw from the same emotional geography.

García Márquez lived in Cartagena intermittently and wrote his final major novel, Love in the Time of Cholera, as a sustained act of imagination about what the city had been in the late nineteenth century.

Love in the Time of Cholera uses the city as a physical argument — the old colonial port as a place where obsession, time, and the persistence of feeling can be treated as serious subjects rather than sentimental ones. The wharves, the old quarter, the smell of the river, the social hierarchy of families who had been important for centuries — García Márquez knew this material from the inside. After his death in 2014, his ashes were interred in Cartagena's cloister of La Merced, a deliberate choice to bury him in the city that his most explicitly romantic novel had claimed.

The City That Persisted

Cartagena's contemporary form is a collision of different pressures that the city has not fully resolved and may never need to. The old city inside the walls is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a major tourist destination. Getsemaní, the neighborhood just outside the walls where enslaved and free people of color lived during the colonial period, has spent the last two decades going from genuine working-class community to contested bohemian territory — murals and small restaurants appearing alongside families who have been there for generations. The beaches at Bocagrande, south of the old city on a long spit of land, are a separate world: high-rise hotels, weekend tourism from Bogotá, the kind of beach resort that could be anywhere in Latin America if you removed the backdrop of the old city walls visible across the bay.

The Caribbean heat — consistent, sometimes relentless, moderated only slightly by sea breezes in the late afternoon — is not incidental to what Cartagena is. It shapes when people move, how buildings are designed, what the streets feel like at noon versus six in the evening. The city that persisted through sieges, reconquest, and a century of economic decline persisted partly because its climate demanded a particular pace. That pace, and the physical form of the old city that grew around it, is what makes Cartagena feel distinct — not just a historic city, but one that has arranged its history in a way that still makes sense in the present.
